cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.summary: Within the gate of a walled city, Christ, with a cross-nimbus, sits on a blue globe and blesses, while a group of crowned kings and armed men approach from the left, one of them pointing toward him. The psalm praises Mount Sion, 'the city of the great King', where 'the kings were assembled' and marvelled.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts-stuttgart-psalter-psalm-.notes: Image from the WLB digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark), showing the whole page with the miniature.

cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.summary: On the left a group of men stand crowded together across a dark hill, and on the right a haloed Christ in an orange mantle stretches out his arm toward them. The scene illustrates the verse just above, 'declinate a me maligni' — 'depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep the commandments of my God'.
facts: The Stuttgart Psalter was made around 820–830 at the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés near Paris; its 168 leaves contain the psalms with 316 coloured miniatures set between the verses they illustrate.
Its pictures interpret the psalms literally, historically or — very often — Christologically, as prophecies of the life of Christ.
cur:manuscripts2-stuttgart-psalter-psalm.notes: The haloed figure is identified as Christ following the psalter's convention; he could also be read as the psalmist speaking. The image is the full page; the miniature occupies only part of it.

cur:monumental2-san-vincenzo-first-bath.summary: The newborn Christ, a sturdy child with a golden cross-nimbus, sits upright in a large footed basin shaped like a chalice, while a midwife seated at the left tests the water and a second woman at the right pours from a jug. Part of the crypt's Nativity, the scene's eucharistic overtones – the Child in a chalice-like font – would have been clear to the monks who prayed here.
facts: The bathing of the Child by midwives comes from apocryphal tradition and was a standard part of Nativity images in both Byzantine and Western early medieval art.

vam:O88110.summary: This small ivory casket is carved on every side with the story of Christ's Passion and Resurrection: the Last Supper on the front, Christ before Herod and the Betrayal on the back, the Agony in the Garden and the Crucifixion on the ends, and on the lid the holy women at the tomb and the Harrowing of Hell. The front, shown here, presents the apostles gathered at a long table with Christ, framed by acanthus borders and later gilt-metal straps.
facts: Its small size and the Last Supper placed on the front suggest, according to the V&A, that it was made as a Eucharistic vessel to hold the unconsecrated host.
The gilt-metal mounts date from about the 12th century, while the hinges and lock are modern.
It belongs to a group of ivories probably from the same workshop, including the V&A's Passion plaque 1-1872 and a panel in Essen; it was in the Farrer collection, sold at Christie's on 13 June 1866.
